notes.title: Dev Diary: Learned Jobs, Lost Frames, Gained Wisdom
notes.notes:
Tried rewriting with Unity’s Job System, but because the data set was small, it ended up slower, so I rolled everything back.
In short: no actual changes.

⸻⸻⸻⸻⸻⸻⸻⸻⸻

Recently, I heard about Unity’s new multithreaded system: Jobs + Entities, supposedly offering speed boosts of 10x, even up to 200x.
I had no idea what it was, but it looked really complicated.

I asked an AI how long it’d take to learn.
It said “half a year,” and I panicked — thought it was going to be math-class levels of pain.

I hesitated for a long time, mentally preparing myself, before I started.
And of course… turns out the AI was confidently lying again.
It didn’t take nearly that long.

That said — yeah, the beginning was full of pain.
Certain Unity packages just wouldn’t install.
I tried importing tutorial files and was greeted with a full-screen wall of error messages.

But I didn’t fall apart sobbing. (Crying wouldn’t help anyway, right?)
Whenever I got too tired, I’d just go watch some funny shows. Then once I felt better, I’d come back and keep learning.

To be honest, the learning process was so hard that I ended up watching a lot of shows. I even wrote a full psychological breakdown of both the protagonist and the villain — just checked: 28,370 words.
It felt like school again — making zero progress in the textbook, but remembering every joke the teacher told in vivid detail.

⸻

Eventually, I finally got the hang of it. I rewrote the “find nearest item” logic using Jobs…
…and the game got slower.

Sometimes dropping to 20 FPS, which is really bad.
Before the rewrite, it was holding steady at 80+ FPS.

That’s when I realized: NativeArray comes with overhead.
For small data sets, it actually hurts performance.

So… I rolled it back.
Still, not a total waste — I learned something that might help with the next game.

⸻

If you’re curious what I’ve been learning, here’s the Unity official documentation:
https://learn.unity.com/course/basics-dots-jobs-entities/tutorial/get-started-with-unitys-job-system

notes.title: Game Update: Bunny Optimization + Mesh Merge
notes.notes:
No need to open if you're an old player — no gameplay changes.
I've refactored part of the bunny code and merged their meshes to improve performance.

------------------------------
I reduced the number of skinned meshes, and the game runs faster now.
It was a painful and tedious process, but I did learn some new things.
Maybe the next game will be better because of it.
I’m honestly afraid all three of my games will get the same kind of comments — that would make it seem like I haven’t improved at all over the years.

------------------------------

Performance Stats
Before (initial version):
• Visible skinned meshes: 298
• Animator components playing: 250

After converting flower animation from bone-based to shader vertex animation:
• Visible skinned meshes: 152
• Animator components playing: 208

After today's bunny mesh merge:
• Visible skinned meshes: 91
• Animator components playing: 43

------------------------------

I finally merged the bunny meshes. And then I remembered why I didn’t do it before.

Having a bunch of scattered small mesh parts is terrible for runtime efficiency,
but it’s great for development — quick to iterate.
Once the mesh is merged, every small adjustment (weighting issues, modeling errors, export problems, adding a new accessory, etc.) requires re-assigning all 25+ materials from scratch.
After doing that a few times, I nearly lost my mind — groundhog screaming noises included.
But screaming doesn’t help, so I kept dragging materials.

Eventually, I thought of numbering the materials to make reassigning them in order easier.

Also, exporting directly from Blender to Unity sometimes just... fails.
Now I export the FBX manually, then drag it into Unity.
Even with numbered materials, doing this over and over is frustrating.
Then I discovered something: if I delete the old FBX but keep its `.meta` file, and reimport a new FBX with the same filename, Unity keeps the material assignments.

No idea why I hadn’t thought of that earlier.
It reminded me of how, as a kid, Chinese homework, when I had to copy homework twice, I’d hold two pens and write both at the same time.
Turns out lots of classmates did that too — or used carbon paper.
Experienced devs are just better at skipping unnecessary steps.

------------------------------

Development is Pain

Some bugs are systemic — they only stop biting you once you’ve been bitten a few times.
Even if I switched engines or 3D software, I’d just run into different bugs.
You just get better at dodging them with time.

------------------------------

I still remember waiting forever for my game’s first ever review.
The player was nice and gave it a positive rating,
but also mentioned the game was poorly optimized.
(Later they deleted the review — maybe they were worried it would hurt my feelings?)

Back then, I had no idea what "optimization" meant.
None of the “anyone can make a game” tutorials talked about it.

3 years later, I think I finally understand what that comment meant.

------------------------------

For example:

• I modeled the bunny and exported it as-is. If it worked, great.
• I didn’t think ahead — now that there are tons of bunny outfits, I can’t even tell which file was the original.
• I threw materials into the scene however I liked.
Now there are hundreds of them scattered around.
Trying to optimize textures and reduce draw calls now is a huge task.

I hope I can avoid all this next time.

---

What’s Next
I want to rewrite the bunny system with a more efficient architecture…
but I don’t know how yet.
I’ve started watching some video tutorials — hopefully I’ll get there.

------------------------------
That'all for chatting. Thanks for being my playper.

notes.title: Minor Performance Improvement Converted bone animation to vertex animation
notes.notes:
Lately, I’ve been working on improving performance. The game had too many bone animations, which really slowed things down. One of the biggest culprits was the large blooming tree.

I rewrote the flower animation using shaders and vertex animation instead of bones—each petal now rotates around its axis via math, not rigging. It runs much faster now and even has fewer vertices!

But then came the pain:
After spending forever on the math, I imported it from Blender to Unity… and everything broke.
Blender uses Z-up, Unity uses Y-up. Local axes flipped. My flower animation exploded. Petals stretched wildly due to bad vertex data. I almost cried 😭

I thought I had finally fixed it… until I ticked “Static” and all the flowers exploded again. Turns out, when you mark something as Static and check "Batching Static", Unity changes the local coordinate system to optimize draw calls—which ruins vertex animation.
Nobody warned me about that! Everyone says "game dev is easy to get into"—but no one mentions this stuff.

Anyway, I unchecked “Batching Static” and the flower animation finally works. Phew.

This small change improved performance a bit. If I can optimize bunny animations and models too, the game could run even better—but for now, I have no idea how. Maybe someday.

notes.title: The pig is back, fixed a bug with Bunny's clothing.
notes.notes:
The pig is back, fixed a bug with Bunny's clothing.
Fixed bird AI, previously it stayed in place if too far from the rabbit.
Added the pig back, summoning the pig doesn't consume anything.

—————— You don’t need to read anything below. That's just for chatting:——————

Originally, I planed Pig to destroy all enemies on the island. Later, I thought Bunnies need to practice fighting monsters. This way, when Pig is not around, Bunnies can protect themselves.

I hope the cute animals can live happily. So, the self-defense ability of Bunny is also important. Even when not working, Bunnies will work hard to stay fit, and no one can bully them.

Pig is not just added back directly; I refactored the code, so it took some extra time.

The NPC's AI part is quite challenging to write. NPC interaction behavior is also the most enjoyable part of the game. For example, I wrote Bunnies run away if they can't win (based on stamina), but if they can win, they run towards the enemy. In actual situations, as they fight, Bunnies might start losing, and then they run away while still trying to hit the enemy, which is quite funny.

As the code progresses, I realized the commonality in the behavior of Bunnies, Pig, and birds (enemies), so I split the old code and refactored it multiple times. Some concepts may be a bit challenging to learn directly (especially for non-computer science professionals like me), but by doing practical examples multiple times, it becomes easier to understand.

Let me describe this state for you. It's like an amateur building houses by hand. These houses are imaginative, with very distinctive shapes and styles, but they are also prone to collapse. Some get blown down by the wind, and some are forcibly demolished because they don't meet building regulations and aren't safe to live in. Suppose this amateur builder repeats this process N times, improving each time after being demolished, reading the building regulations. In that case, they gradually approach the standard acceptance level.

It's somewhat like this. I repeatedly refactor the code, although it's tiring, but the code becomes much clearer and easier to maintain.

Each code refactoring is like rewriting the code, bringing unknown new bugs. Some bugs, I didn't anticipate at all, were triggered by external factors. 

For example, upgrading Blender from version 3 to 4 is a good thing. I like Blender 4.0; the Geometry node functionality is more powerful. However, if I use Blender 4, I can't continue modifying the animations I made in Blender 3. I've done too many animations to give up. I initially thought of continuing to animate with Blender 3 and modeling with Blender 4. Today I noticed that if I choose Blender 3, and then drag Blender 4 source files into Unity, some model will disappear. Currently, I can only use both Blender 3 and 4 simultaneously and remember which version to open for what purpose.

For example, upgrading the Unity editor, all previews of materials and models disappeared. No wonder industry professionals often upgrade the software last... after others have gone through all the pitfalls caused by the upgrade. In the future, I probably won't choose the newest software version but the second newest.

Early on, when looking at player screenshots, I was confused for a long time. 
I carefully adjusted settings such as sunlight, colors, etc., but in some player screenshots, these adjustments weren't reflected at all. Later, I realized that different graphics cards and screens result in different rendering results. I can't make players truly "see" the visual effects exactly like on my computer. But this is my first game, and I just wanted it to look good. It was a somewhat understandable mistake.

The main refund reasons for this game are: 
not fun.
the frame rate is too slow. 

My computer configuration is quite good, and the HDRP runs at 60 frames per second. If changed to URP, it can run at 140 frames per second. 
After all, it's an interactive game, not just an animation. Smooth gameplay is the most important. 
The next game will use URP, and the speed will be much faster than this game, and I will try to design better gameplay. URP is very fast, and although its visuals can't compare with HDRP, but most machines can play it smoothly. Currently, HDRP requires a relatively good computer to play.
My next game plan has also been overturned many times, and the game title may change. 

That's all.

The hardest part of making a game is not art or code, although those are difficult too. The hardest part is how to make a game fun. The answer to that is not so easy.
To make the game more fun, I've tried various things. Adding more animations to the bunny is the easiest thing to do. It doesn't require much code modification, just keep adding animations. But it's not enough to keep players engaged for a long time. So I often try to modify the gameplay.

However, frequently modifying the game often means starting over and redoing a lot of work. Many times, after spending a lot of time writing a feature, I end up deleting it because it's not necessary or doesn't add to the fun of the game.

For example, recently I wrote a feature that allowed users to change the map and build their own island. It took a lot of effort to develop and test, but after playing around with it, I found that it didn't make the game more fun, and the built terrain didn't look as good as the original islands. Plus, it made the game and controls more complicated. So I removed the map feature and rolled back to the old code. 

Developing this way, creating something, testing it out, and then deciding whether to include it in the game is a very costly habit. Luckily, I'm the only developer on this project, and I can only imagine the frustration others would feel.
I wanted to show you a video of the map feature, but some people (who don’t like reading only watch videos) might think the map feature was a new addition and complain about not being able to find it in the game, so I won't bother.

Also, this is my first game, and I come from an art background. The code complexity has slowly surpassed my abilities. The reasonable approach is to ignore some bugs as long as the code still works, and focus on the art and animations. That way, there will always be a playable game.

But when you can't understand a bug, no matter how much you try to debug it, you can't find the cause. At that point, you can't give up and have to enter survival mode. The more you think about the bug, the more it seems like it shouldn't even be happening. It's a singularity, a mystery, the beginning of a mysterious world, and an indication of another plot in life. 
I dreamt of possible causes for the bug nonstop. I just can’t let it go. I have to solve this bug. Fortunately, after trying various things, I finally located and fixed the problem! I could finally sleep peacefully. 
After solving it, it turned out to be a mundane, ordinary bug, not worth mentioning. 

Some developers don't fix bugs, not because they don't care about users, but because some bugs are beyond their technical abilities. When developing independently, it's difficult to balance code and art, and some aspects are hard to achieve perfection.

Finally, I noticed several players saying that they couldn't rotate the camera. Is it because they don't know how to use it (interaction prompts are not clear) or because there is a problem with the code (camera rotation and translation are not working properly)? 

To rotate the camera, use the right mouse button and drag it. Use the left or middle mouse button to translate the camera. I tested it on multiple machines, and it works fine. I already checked the camera code, but since I couldn't reproduce the camera issue, I made some changes based on guesses that might cause the problem. I also added a reset camera button at the top. 

If you have any suggestions related to the camera or have encountered any issues, please leave a message for feedback~ 
It would be better if you could record or take screenshots. That way, I can see where the problem lies.

After fighting with the bug for a long time, I suddenly realized that you might not believe that I really fought and won the bug when I submit the new version. After all, you can't see much change from the game interface. Just like "The Old Man and the Sea," even though I won the battle, I didn't get any loot, just exhaustion and a story. So I added a small animation of a bunny holding a pinwheel. So you can see some changes.

That's about it. Thank you for reading.

notes.title: changed mushroom factory, refactored bunny job, add more bunny story letter
notes.notes:
1. Refactored some of the code in the bunny work section.
2. When the bunny workers are idle, they will help movers.
3. Rebuilt the model of the mushroom factory.
4. Added some letters written by the bunnies.
5. Modified the logic for the bunnies’' eating behavior, dividing it into main meals (which can make them full) and snacks (which can make them happy, but not full).
6. Fixed a bug where the bunny work state would be incorrect when reloading a new file.
7. Made some small changes, such as modifying the display of numbers, removing some building ground, and changing some textures.

In this version, I continued to refactor the code for the rabbit work section. It was a process where bugs kept knocking me down, but I couldn't give up. At least not today! Fortunately, I managed to fix everything in the end.

I also redesigned the mushroom factory and added some letters written by the small rabbits. Initially, the bunny letters were just an Easter egg design, but I was pleasantly surprised to find that you all enjoyed this part. So I add more letters.

After being beaten up by the code for a while, it was really pleasant to return to my familiar fields of modeling, animation, and art. I removed some of the building ground to avoid players feeling compelled to align everything perfectly. 

I had originally planned to change the map to a hexagonal grid, but realized that it would require too much overall model changes and code modifications, so I decided to postpone it for now.

I revisited some notes I wrote during the early stages of game design. The code section went through multiple revisions. Initially, it was just a vague concept, but after making the game and interacting with user comments, many ideas gradually took shape. Today, I found that my handwritten notes had become quite thick. Only after doing it myself did I realize the difficulties of indie game development. 

Many comments encouraged me to keep going and expressed concerns that the project might be abandoned prematurely. Independent game development is much harder than I had imagined. Even after 5 months, the total revenue from my game is not enough to cover a month's electricity bill. I understand why some people give up on maintaining their projects, but I will try my best to keep going for as long as I can.

There are also happy moments, which are why many people persist in making independent games, independent films, and so on. Creative freedom is truly joyful! Seeing the bunnies running around and living happily on the island makes me very happy. 
That's all for this update. 

I've always hoped to make the game more fun, so thank you for your comments and feedback. 
With everyone's help, the game has become much more enjoyable than it was during the first month of release. 
If you have any ideas or suggestions, please leave them in the comments. 
Thank you!!

notes.title: Refactored code, update night scenes, and some UI
notes.notes:
Thank you for your sincere message. 
I was also a bit surprised to see that people are actually paying attention to the updates. 
I often wait a long time for a new message and sometimes worry that I'm just talking to the air.

Getting feedback is a pleasant surprise, especially when someone points out specific issues in the game. It shows that someone is actually playing it! 
I'm so happy about that! My first reaction was to climb onto the roof and shout, "Someone is playing my game!" 
But... I have to fix the bugs and continue writing code first.

Game design is fun, but the implementation process is painful and time-consuming. 
I design happily, but then I have a furrowed brow when it comes to implementation.

For this update, I updated some UI and added night lighting to some of the buildings.
I also refactored part of the code. 
This was a painful and time-consuming process, but it was worth it. 

I don't know if you guys play Jenga or not. 
As a novice game designer (like me), I often just write functions directly, like making the bunny run, sleep, eat, and so on. Gradually, the unstable blocks pile up higher and higher. 
Players may not realize it, but I know that the project is about to collapse. 

So I have to stop and spend a lot of time refactoring the code. Although players can't see the difference, they can see the new features that have been added. 

Finally, the refactoring is done. I played it myself and didn't encounter any bugs. 
This was a big change, so there may be some overlooked bugs that I didn't find during testing. Please leave a message and let me know. 

Thank you.
